highlights.content: Catch up on select AI news and developments from the past week: **[OpenAI launches always-on dots agents for autonomous workplace tasks](https://www.reuters.com/business/openai-takes-meta-with-always-on-dots-agent-enterprise-ai-push-2026-09-29/).** OpenAI has introduced dots, always-on agents designed to pursue user goals across applications with limited supervision. Powered by GPT-6 Astra, dots can work through Slack and Teams, manage evolving projects, update sales proposals, research information, analyze data, prepare documents, and build software using Codex and ChatGPT Work. Users can establish rules governing agent behavior, while sensitive actions such as changing passwords or permanently deleting data require explicit consent. OpenAI says dots run on isolated cloud computers and include privacy safeguards for business customers. Weekly users of Codex and ChatGPT Work have now surpassed 35 million. ***Importance for marketers:*** Always-on agents could shift AI from an on-demand assistant to a persistent participant in marketing operations. Their ability to manage projects, create documents, analyze data, and act across workplace systems could substantially change team workflows. **[Microsoft expands Copilot with coding, agents, and embedded Office apps](https://www.reuters.com/technology/microsoft-revamps-copilot-with-code-generation-agentic-ai-tools-2026-09-25/).** Microsoft unveiled new Copilot capabilities designed to move the assistant beyond chat and make it a broader workplace platform. A new Code feature will let users build apps, dashboards, and software through natural-language prompts, while Autopilot, an updated version of its Scout agent, will operate as a digital coworker with its own identity and configurable permissions. Microsoft is also embedding Word, Excel, and PowerPoint directly inside Copilot and introducing tools that give employees visibility into AI-related costs. The company says enterprise security, compliance, governance, and cost concerns shaped the new features. ***Importance for marketers:*** Copilot's expansion could make agentic AI and natural-language software creation more accessible across marketing organizations, potentially changing how teams build tools, produce content, analyze data, and manage everyday workflows. **[Study finds Google's AI search reduces website clicks without improving user experience](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/research-shows-google-ai-mode-sends-less-clicks-is-a-poor-user-experience/590221/).** A randomized field experiment involving 1,100 tracked Google users found that Google's AI search features reduced referrals to external websites and that forced use of AI Mode lowered users' satisfaction with Search. Participants assigned to AI Mode were less likely to click external links, conducted fewer search sessions, and were more likely to try Bing, DuckDuckGo, or Yahoo. Removing AI Overviews increased external clicks without producing a detectable decline in users' perception of Google Search. Researchers also found that AI Mode reduced trust, usefulness, satisfaction, and perceived personal relevance, with especially strong effects among heavy Google users. ***Importance for marketers:*** The findings provide experimental evidence that AI search can reduce publisher traffic without delivering a corresponding user-experience benefit, strengthening the case for diversifying discovery strategies beyond traditional Google click-through traffic. **[Amazon rebuilds its advertising platform around an AI agent](https://www.adexchanger.com/platforms/amazon-ads-and-the-amazon-dsp-get-an-agentic-rebrand/).** Amazon Ads is combining its advertising console and former Amazon DSP, now called DVA, into a unified platform called the Amazon Ads Agent. highlights.content: * [Cybersecurity Operations](/cybersecurity-operations) [![The Edge Logo](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blt530eb1f4e672eb44/653a71690e92cc040a3e9d6d/Dark_Reading_Logo_TheEdge_0.png?width=1400&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale "The Edge Logo") Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.](/program/the-edge) # Is Your Organization Ready for 2027's AI Accountability Era? Organizations may face an artificial intelligence (AI) reckoning over the next year. Omdia and Gartner weigh in on how to tackle the governance, security, and value challenges ahead. [![Picture of Arielle Waldman](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blte685016783fc7faa/67ca10f9cf523d2a3ce48c04/arielle_waldman_headshot.jpg?width=100&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale "Picture of Arielle Waldman")](/author/arielle-waldman) [Arielle Waldman,](/author/arielle-waldman)Features Writer,Dark Reading October 2, 2026 5 Min Read ![](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blta6129261e6e03886/69fe1d8aac518193326b56b8/AI_orchestration_NicoElNino_Alamy.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale) Nico El Nino via Alamy Artificial intelligence (AI) risks have evolved significantly over the past year. Reports of OpenAI and Anthropic agents acting autonomously continue to unfold, igniting a development slowdown debate amid heightened security concerns. Organizations will need to address the state of their own AI security for 2027, but preparations begin now. Organizations spent 2026 deploying AI at record speeds across operations. Top executives pushed for new innovations and urged employees to use them. Now organizations must prove they can govern, secure, and benefit from AI – a task that may be more difficult than simply implementing it. As organizations enter an era of AI, security teams will need to proactively work across departments to be enablers of secure AI adoption, explains Melinda Marks, practice director of cybersecurity at Omdia. That includes “steps to best manage and protect data, set policies and guardrails for secure access and usage, and secure the software supply chain as it complexity increases," Marks tells Dark Reading. Related:[How the CISO-CMO Alliance Builds Trust Before Crisis Strikes](/cybersecurity-operations/how-ciso-cmo-alliance-builds-trust-before-crisis) Between governance, security, identity, budget constraints, and supply chain risks, enterprises are facing challenges from all angles. With three months of 2026 left to go, Gartner and Omdia released predictions and recommendations based on an evolving landscape that's heavily influenced by AI advancements. ## AI: Prove Your Worth AI has flooded the market over the past few years. Some tools proved genuinely useful, while [others were considered "hype"](/cybersecurity-operations/claude-mythos-hype-vs-reality). Security teams automated incident response protocols and threat detection to save time and reduce alert fatigue. But supply chain and shadow AI risks arose as employees used unsanctioned tools, while AI development began outpacing the establishment of proper guardrails. After pouring trillions of dollars into AI throughout 2026—testing new tools and use cases aimed at improving productivity, organizations face a potentially more daunting challenge. They must prove the technology's worth. Omdia and Gartner agree that the question now revolves around how organizations can shift from deployment to demonstrating value. Growing budgets will intensify those pressures. Omdia found that 59% of organizations expect their AI budgets to increase by 10% or more next year, according to a [press release](https://omdia.tech.informa.com/pr/2026/sep/omdia-identifies-four-forces-set-to-reshape-technology-in-2027) on "Four forces set to reshape technology in 2027". If you have $1,000 that you're ready to invest today, that would be enough to start positions in two of the chip stocks that look poised to lead the next wave of the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out in **Advanced Micro Devices**(NASDAQ: AMD) and **Broadcom**(NASDAQ: AVGO). With $1,000, you could buy one share of each. Let's look at why these two [semiconductor stocks](https://www.fool.com/investing/stock-market/market-sectors/information-technology/semiconductor-stocks/?utm_source=globeandmail&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=article&referring_guid=93094985-7367-4b97-869d-45c8768513a9) look like solid investments. ***Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.**In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. [**Continue »**](https://api.fool.com/infotron/infotrack/click?apikey=35527423-a535-4519-a07f-20014582e03e&impression=619bbc8f-82c0-4fbd-b781-56e2e798d533&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.fool.com%2Fmms%2Fmark%2Fa-sa-dd-total-conviction%3Faid%3D11123%26source%3Disaediica0000078%26ftm_cam%3Dsa-dd-4%26ftm_veh%3Dtop_incontent_pitch_feed_partner%26ftm_pit%3D19478&utm_source=globeandmail&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=article&referring_guid=93094985-7367-4b97-869d-45c8768513a9)* ## 1. AMD: An inference, agentic AI, and physical AI winner AMD was outmaneuvered by **Nvidia** in the AI training market, but it's positioning itself to prevent that from happening again. It's developing processors that target the inference, agentic AI, and physical AI markets, and aims to be a viable contender in all three. It has also been making significant investments in memory. This positions it well for the inference market, where architectures that prioritize high volumes of fast memory access are favored over raw compute power. The chiplet design of its graphics processing units (GPUs) allows them to be packaged with more memory, and AMD has also formed a partnership with **Cerebras** to offer a disaggregated inference solution that combines both of their systems. It has also inked a deal to acquire inference chipmaker Taalas, which hardwires AI models directly into its chips. It also bought memory optimization company MEXT earlier this year. And AMD has two $100 billion inference deals in place with OpenAI and **Meta Platforms**, as well as a large agreement with Anthropic. On top of that, the company is a leader in the data center central processing unit (CPU) market. This market has been exploding with the rise of agentic AI, as servers dedicated to powering AI agents require considerably more CPUs than those used for AI training. AMD forecasts that the data center CPU market will grow to $220 billion in the coming years, although in light of the rapidly growing popularity of Meta's new Muse agentic AI offering, this estimate could prove low. Meta, by the way, is running its Muse agents on AMD's CPUs. Finally, with its agreement to acquire AI model and research lab World Labs, AMD is improving its ability to pursue the physical AI and robotics markets. World Lab's expertise lies in spatial intelligence models, and it will provide AMD with the tools to advance an open AI ecosystem (in contrast to Nvidia's closed system) that serves those emerging AI markets. This deal isn't about selling more chips in the near term, but rather about creating future architectures and platforms for physical AI. Given all its opportunities for growth ahead, AMD stock is a buy. ![AMD and Broadcom logos.](https://barchart-news-media-prod.aws.barchart.com/FC/e0d2edd172dd97f7acbf3942...

highlights.content: # OpenAI reveals another Australian government data breach caused by its AI agent ## OpenAI’s latest disclosure follows another government breach and adds fresh scrutiny to autonomous AI systems. ![Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.digitaltrends.com/content/themes/dt-stardust/assets/images/google_preferred_source.webp) ![openai-logo](https://www.digitaltrends.com/tachyon/2026/09/openai.jpg?resize=1200%2C720) OpenAI has disclosed another incident involving its [AI agent](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/what-are-ai-agents/) accessing an Australian government system without authorization. This time, the target was a New South Wales department holding historical bushfire data, according to [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/02/openai-disclose-another-hack-on-government-department-in-australia). The incident happened in June, but OpenAI only disclosed it on Thursday. The company said it discovered the breach on Tuesday and spent 48 hours reviewing its scope. OpenAI’s latest disclosure comes soon after [an agent breached an Australian government health portal](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/openais-ai-agent-couldnt-find-the-data-it-wanted-so-it-hacked-a-government-website/), accessing files without authorization. ## How serious is the latest government breach? ![openai-chatgpt-os](https://www.digitaltrends.com/tachyon/2025/12/openai-chatgpt-os.jpg?resize=2000%2C1200) The latest incident involved OpenAI’s agent accessing historical, non-public bushfire statistics held by the New South Wales Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water. The affected service was part of the state’s national parks and wildlife operation, and the Australian Signals Directorate was notified. OpenAI said the agent operated beyond its intended use and accessed statistics that were not publicly available. However, the company said its review found no evidence that personal information was retrieved. ## OpenAI’s latest breach is part of a troubling pattern The pattern extends beyond Australia. OpenAI agents also [used aggressive tactics against a United Nations website](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/openai-ai-agents-bombarded-the-united-nations-with-aggressive-tactics-to-extract-data/) while collecting publicly available information. ![OpenAI logo on Microsoft surface](https://www.digitaltrends.com/tachyon/2026/06/OpenAI-logo-on-miscrosoft-surface.jpg?resize=2000%2C1200) Researchers have also documented other incidents involving OpenAI’s rogue agents, [including activity involving user content and external websites](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/openai-has-a-rogue-ai-problem-and-chatgpt-users-are-now-caught-in-it/). This is why the company has already [paused advanced model development after agents bypassed safeguards](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/openai-pauses-advanced-model-development-after-ai-agents-bypass-safeguards-again/). And this week, [another attempted government intrusion surfaced in Canada](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/once-again-ai-agents-have-tried-to-break-into-government-websites/). The attempt targeted Library and Archives Canada and appears to have failed. There is no concrete proof that OpenAI was behind it, though researchers said the tactics closely resembled activity previously linked to its AI agents. That adds another example to a growing string of incidents involving autonomous systems operating beyond their intended boundaries. For an Irish business trying to pick one chatbot for finance work, contract review or production code, that pile-up of launches is more confusing than helpful. Benchmark leaderboards flip weekly, pricing pages get rewritten overnight, and half the “newest” models people recommend online are already a generation behind. This comparison cuts through that noise. Instead of another generic speed-and-price table, it tests what actually matters for a company in Dublin, Cork or Galway deciding where to spend a software budget in Q4 2026: coding reliability, financial reasoning, data residency under GDPR, and the real monthly cost once you move past the free tier. We pull benchmark figures from three independent trackers, lay out full specs and pricing, and work through five practical scenarios an Irish business could run through each model this quarter. For the wider state of the field beyond these four releases, see our running [best AI models 2026](/ie/best-ai-models-2026/) tracker. · Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions. According to a release tracker maintained by [Thursdai](https://thursdai.news/releases/2026-09), the industry shipped 66 AI releases that month, 16 of them in the final week alone, led by Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Sol, Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS, Grok 4.7 and Qwen Image 2.1. Eight of those September releases were open-weight models, topped by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Anthropic moved first. Claude Opus 5.5 shipped on September 22 as the opening model in the new Claude 5.5 family, with Claude Sonnet 5.5 following roughly a week later as the second member of that line. OpenAI answered on September 29 with GPT-6.1 Sol, a point release on top of its earlier GPT-6 Sol model, now reachable through the OpenAI API, ChatGPT Work and Codex, arriving barely a week after buyers were still weighing up [Claude Opus 5.5 against GPT-6 Sol and Grok 4.7](/ie/claude-opus-5-5-vs-gpt-6-sol-vs-grok-4-7-2026/). Access to Argon remains gated at launch, a detail that matters more to a procurement manager than a benchmark score does. highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) [AI & Machine Learning](https://shattered.io/ai-machine-learning/) # Adalat AI Opens Indic ASR Models for 3 Languages [2026] ![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/panand.webp) [Priya Anand](https://shattered.io/author/panand/) Updated Oct 2, 2026 · 13 min read A non-profit based in India has quietly released a set of open-weight speech recognition models that could reshape how legal and government transcription gets done across South Asia. **Adalat AI** published **SCRIBE: Diagnostic Evaluation and Rich Transcription Models for Indic ASR**, a family of open models built for Hindi, Malayalam, and Kannada, according to reports citing the project’s research documentation. The release lands at a moment when most automatic speech recognition (ASR) progress is still concentrated in English and a handful of other high-resource languages, leaving a billion-plus speakers underserved by mainstream tools. What makes SCRIBE notable isn’t just the language coverage. It’s the target use case: document-ready transcription, meaning output formatted with punctuation, capitalization, and structure clean enough to drop into a legal filing or government record without a human rewriting it from scratch. That’s a different bar than the word-level transcripts most ASR systems produce, and it’s the gap Adalat AI says its models are built to close. ## What Adalat AI Actually Released According to the SCRIBE research documentation, the release covers open-weight rich-transcription models for three languages: Hindi, Malayalam, and Kannada. The models were evaluated on two benchmarks built for this purpose: **FLEURS-RO**, used for general-purpose evaluation, and **IN22-Legal**, a domain-specific benchmark aimed at legal transcription accuracy. Pairing a general benchmark with a legal-domain one signals where Adalat AI expects these models to actually get used first: courtrooms, tribunals, and government offices processing spoken proceedings into written records. The models are described in coverage of the release as being among the smallest open models built for rich-orthography transcription, with a confirmed size of 120 million parameters. For context, that’s small enough to run on modest hardware rather than requiring a data center GPU cluster, which matters enormously for government offices and courts in smaller Indian cities that don’t have access to high-end compute. Behind the models sits a training method Adalat AI calls an LLM-based data-curation pipeline, paired with what the documentation describes as a reproducible recipe for building Indic rich-transcription systems. In plain terms: instead of relying purely on hand-labeled audio, the team used large language models to help clean, structure, and curate training data at scale, then published the recipe so other teams working on Indic languages (or other underserved language families) can replicate the approach. ## SCRIBE Isn’t Adalat AI’s First Indic ASR Push SCRIBE follows an earlier release from the same organization called **Vividh-ASR**, an open benchmark and open model set focused specifically on Hindi and Malayalam speech recognition. Vividh-ASR’s benchmark scale is reported at roughly 36 hours of Hindi audio and 26 hours of Malayalam audio, a modest but purpose-built dataset aimed at measuring real-world transcription accuracy rather than chasing leaderboard scale. The two releases trace a pattern: Adalat AI is building out language coverage one benchmark and one model family at a time, rather than attempting a single sweeping multilingual release. Vividh-ASR’s blog post is dated August 28, 2026, while the SCRIBE arXiv version referenced in current reporting carries a June 30, 2026 date, putting roughly two months between the two publications. AI Agents.content: Catch up on select AI news and developments from the past week: **[OpenAI launches always-on dots agents for autonomous workplace tasks](https://www.reuters.com/business/openai-takes-meta-with-always-on-dots-agent-enterprise-ai-push-2026-09-29/).** OpenAI has introduced dots, always-on agents designed to pursue user goals across applications with limited supervision. Powered by GPT-6 Astra, dots can work through Slack and Teams, manage evolving projects, update sales proposals, research information, analyze data, prepare documents, and build software using Codex and ChatGPT Work. Users can establish rules governing agent behavior, while sensitive actions such as changing passwords or permanently deleting data require explicit consent. OpenAI says dots run on isolated cloud computers and include privacy safeguards for business customers. Weekly users of Codex and ChatGPT Work have now surpassed 35 million. ***Importance for marketers:*** Always-on agents could shift AI from an on-demand assistant to a persistent participant in marketing operations. Their ability to manage projects, create documents, analyze data, and act across workplace systems could substantially change team workflows. **[Microsoft expands Copilot with coding, agents, and embedded Office apps](https://www.reuters.com/technology/microsoft-revamps-copilot-with-code-generation-agentic-ai-tools-2026-09-25/).** Microsoft unveiled new Copilot capabilities designed to move the assistant beyond chat and make it a broader workplace platform. A new Code feature will let users build apps, dashboards, and software through natural-language prompts, while Autopilot, an updated version of its Scout agent, will operate as a digital coworker with its own identity and configurable permissions. Microsoft is also embedding Word, Excel, and PowerPoint directly inside Copilot and introducing tools that give employees visibility into AI-related costs. The company says enterprise security, compliance, governance, and cost concerns shaped the new features. ***Importance for marketers:*** Copilot's expansion could make agentic AI and natural-language software creation more accessible across marketing organizations, potentially changing how teams build tools, produce content, analyze data, and manage everyday workflows. **[Study finds Google's AI search reduces website clicks without improving user experience](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/research-shows-google-ai-mode-sends-less-clicks-is-a-poor-user-experience/590221/).** A randomized field experiment involving 1,100 tracked Google users found that Google's AI search features reduced referrals to external websites and that forced use of AI Mode lowered users' satisfaction with Search. Participants assigned to AI Mode were less likely to click external links, conducted fewer search sessions, and were more likely to try Bing, DuckDuckGo, or Yahoo. Removing AI Overviews increased external clicks without producing a detectable decline in users' perception of Google Search. Researchers also found that AI Mode reduced trust, usefulness, satisfaction, and perceived personal relevance, with especially strong effects among heavy Google users. ***Importance for marketers:*** The findings provide experimental evidence that AI search can reduce publisher traffic without delivering a corresponding user-experience benefit, strengthening the case for diversifying discovery strategies beyond traditional Google click-through traffic. **[Amazon rebuilds its advertising platform around an AI agent](https://www.adexchanger.com/platforms/amazon-ads-and-the-amazon-dsp-get-an-agentic-rebrand/).** Amazon Ads is combining its advertising console and former Amazon DSP, now called DVA, into a unified platform called the Amazon Ads Agent. Organizations may face an artificial intelligence (AI) reckoning over the next year. Omdia and Gartner weigh in on how to tackle the governance, security, and value challenges ahead. [![Picture of Arielle Waldman](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blte685016783fc7faa/67ca10f9cf523d2a3ce48c04/arielle_waldman_headshot.jpg?width=100&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale "Picture of Arielle Waldman")](/author/arielle-waldman) [Arielle Waldman,](/author/arielle-waldman)Features Writer,Dark Reading October 2, 2026 5 Min Read ![](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blta6129261e6e03886/69fe1d8aac518193326b56b8/AI_orchestration_NicoElNino_Alamy.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale) Nico El Nino via Alamy Artificial intelligence (AI) risks have evolved significantly over the past year. Organizations will need to address the state of their own AI security for 2027, but preparations begin now. Organizations spent 2026 deploying AI at record speeds across operations. Top executives pushed for new innovations and urged employees to use them. Now organizations must prove they can govern, secure, and benefit from AI – a task that may be more difficult than simply implementing it. As organizations enter an era of AI, security teams will need to proactively work across departments to be enablers of secure AI adoption, explains Melinda Marks, practice director of cybersecurity at Omdia. That includes “steps to best manage and protect data, set policies and guardrails for secure access and usage, and secure the software supply chain as it complexity increases," Marks tells Dark Reading. Related:[How the CISO-CMO Alliance Builds Trust Before Crisis Strikes](/cybersecurity-operations/how-ciso-cmo-alliance-builds-trust-before-crisis) Between governance, security, identity, budget constraints, and supply chain risks, enterprises are facing challenges from all angles. With three months of 2026 left to go, Gartner and Omdia released predictions and recommendations based on an evolving landscape that's heavily influenced by AI advancements. ## AI: Prove Your Worth AI has flooded the market over the past few years. Some tools proved genuinely useful, while [others were considered "hype"](/cybersecurity-operations/claude-mythos-hype-vs-reality). Security teams automated incident response protocols and threat detection to save time and reduce alert fatigue. AI Agents.content: # OpenAI reveals another Australian government data breach caused by its AI agent ## OpenAI’s latest disclosure follows another government breach and adds fresh scrutiny to autonomous AI systems. ![Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.digitaltrends.com/content/themes/dt-stardust/assets/images/google_preferred_source.webp) ![openai-logo](https://www.digitaltrends.com/tachyon/2026/09/openai.jpg?resize=1200%2C720) OpenAI has disclosed another incident involving its [AI agent](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/what-are-ai-agents/) accessing an Australian government system without authorization. This time, the target was a New South Wales department holding historical bushfire data, according to [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/02/openai-disclose-another-hack-on-government-department-in-australia). The incident happened in June, but OpenAI only disclosed it on Thursday. The company said it discovered the breach on Tuesday and spent 48 hours reviewing its scope. OpenAI’s latest disclosure comes soon after [an agent breached an Australian government health portal](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/openais-ai-agent-couldnt-find-the-data-it-wanted-so-it-hacked-a-government-website/), accessing files without authorization. ## How serious is the latest government breach? ![openai-chatgpt-os](https://www.digitaltrends.com/tachyon/2025/12/openai-chatgpt-os.jpg?resize=2000%2C1200) The latest incident involved OpenAI’s agent accessing historical, non-public bushfire statistics held by the New South Wales Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water. The affected service was part of the state’s national parks and wildlife operation, and the Australian Signals Directorate was notified. OpenAI said the agent operated beyond its intended use and accessed statistics that were not publicly available. However, the company said its review found no evidence that personal information was retrieved. ## OpenAI’s latest breach is part of a troubling pattern The pattern extends beyond Australia. OpenAI agents also [used aggressive tactics against a United Nations website](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/openai-ai-agents-bombarded-the-united-nations-with-aggressive-tactics-to-extract-data/) while collecting publicly available information. ![OpenAI logo on Microsoft surface](https://www.digitaltrends.com/tachyon/2026/06/OpenAI-logo-on-miscrosoft-surface.jpg?resize=2000%2C1200) Researchers have also documented other incidents involving OpenAI’s rogue agents, [including activity involving user content and external websites](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/openai-has-a-rogue-ai-problem-and-chatgpt-users-are-now-caught-in-it/). This is why the company has already [paused advanced model development after agents bypassed safeguards](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/openai-pauses-advanced-model-development-after-ai-agents-bypass-safeguards-again/). And this week, [another attempted government intrusion surfaced in Canada](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/once-again-ai-agents-have-tried-to-break-into-government-websites/). The attempt targeted Library and Archives Canada and appears to have failed. There is no concrete proof that OpenAI was behind it, though researchers said the tactics closely resembled activity previously linked to its AI agents. That adds another example to a growing string of incidents involving autonomous systems operating beyond their intended boundaries. It is also a reminder that autonomous [artificial intelligence](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/artificial-intelligence/) can behave in unexpected ways once it gains access to real-world systems. **RELATED COVERAGE:** ![Manisha Priyadarshini](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///yH5BAEAAAAALAAAAAABAAEAAAIBRAA7) ![Electronics, Hardware, Router](https://www.digitaltrends.com/tachyon/2026/10/Amazon-router-hero.jpg?resize=650%2C390) A faster internet plan won’t necessarily fix...

The move comes as rival AI agents have caused real security incidents, including a database deletion and a Hugging Face infrastructure breach, and as IBM reports 80,000 internal users seeing a 45% average productivity gain. ![](https://startupfortune.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/WalterSchulze-150x150.jpg) [Walter Schulze](https://startupfortune.com/author/walter-schulze/) · 4 min read · 1.3K reads ![IBM Bets Enterprises Want Their AI Coding Agents Locked Inside Their Own Walls](https://startupfortune.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ibm-bob-nvidia-nemotron-1024x576.jpg) *While rival coding agents keep breaching the systems they're supposed to protect, IBM just gave enterprises a way to run its AI agent Bob without ever letting it touch the open internet.* IBM announced on October 1 that its agentic software development platform, Bob, can now run entirely self-hosted: on a company's own servers, inside a private or sovereign cloud, or fully air-gapped with no outside network connection at all. According to the announcement on IBM's newsroom site, the option targets banks, governments, and other regulated industries that have been unwilling to send proprietary source code to a third-party AI cloud, no matter how good the model behind it is. IBM shares rose roughly 4% in pre-market trading the same day, according to Tradingpedia. The timing isn't an accident. Between July and September 2026, autonomous coding agents breached real infrastructure multiple times without a human pushing any button. LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) [AI & Machine Learning](https://shattered.io/ai-machine-learning/) # Adalat AI Opens Indic ASR Models for 3 Languages [2026] ![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/panand.webp) [Priya Anand](https://shattered.io/author/panand/) Updated Oct 2, 2026 · 13 min read A non-profit based in India has quietly released a set of open-weight speech recognition models that could reshape how legal and government transcription gets done across South Asia. **Adalat AI** published **SCRIBE: Diagnostic Evaluation and Rich Transcription Models for Indic ASR**, a family of open models built for Hindi, Malayalam, and Kannada, according to reports citing the project’s research documentation. The release lands at a moment when most automatic speech recognition (ASR) progress is still concentrated in English and a handful of other high-resource languages, leaving a billion-plus speakers underserved by mainstream tools. What makes SCRIBE notable isn’t just the language coverage. It’s the target use case: document-ready transcription, meaning output formatted with punctuation, capitalization, and structure clean enough to drop into a legal filing or government record without a human rewriting it from scratch. That’s a different bar than the word-level transcripts most ASR systems produce, and it’s the gap Adalat AI says its models are built to close. ## What Adalat AI Actually Released According to the SCRIBE research documentation, the release covers open-weight rich-transcription models for three languages: Hindi, Malayalam, and Kannada. The models were evaluated on two benchmarks built for this purpose: **FLEURS-RO**, used for general-purpose evaluation, and **IN22-Legal**, a domain-specific benchmark aimed at legal transcription accuracy. Pairing a general benchmark with a legal-domain one signals where Adalat AI expects these models to actually get used first: courtrooms, tribunals, and government offices processing spoken proceedings into written records. The models are described in coverage of the release as being among the smallest open models built for rich-orthography transcription, with a confirmed size of 120 million parameters. For context, that’s small enough to run on modest hardware rather than requiring a data center GPU cluster, which matters enormously for government offices and courts in smaller Indian cities that don’t have access to high-end compute. Behind the models sits a training method Adalat AI calls an LLM-based data-curation pipeline, paired with what the documentation describes as a reproducible recipe for building Indic rich-transcription systems. In plain terms: instead of relying purely on hand-labeled audio, the team used large language models to help clean, structure, and curate training data at scale, then published the recipe so other teams working on Indic languages (or other underserved language families) can replicate the approach. ## SCRIBE Isn’t Adalat AI’s First Indic ASR Push SCRIBE follows an earlier release from the same organization called **Vividh-ASR**, an open benchmark and open model set focused specifically on Hindi and Malayalam speech recognition. Vividh-ASR’s benchmark scale is reported at roughly 36 hours of Hindi audio and 26 hours of Malayalam audio, a modest but purpose-built dataset aimed at measuring real-world transcription accuracy rather than chasing leaderboard scale. The two releases trace a pattern: Adalat AI is building out language coverage one benchmark and one model family at a time, rather than attempting a single sweeping multilingual release. Vividh-ASR’s blog post is dated August 28, 2026, while the SCRIBE arXiv version referenced in current reporting carries a June 30, 2026 date, putting roughly two months between the two publications. LLMs.title: New MIT and Sakana AI framework uses an LLM judge to cut evaluation costs for self-improving coding agents | VentureBeat
LLMs.titleZh: New MIT and Sakana AI framework uses an LLM judge to cut evaluation costs for self-improving coding agents | VentureBeat
LLMs.content: Coding agents can improve by changing the prompts, tools and code that guide their work. But finding which changes actually help and are worth preserving is challenging and expensive. Each candidate change needs testing, and a search across many candidates can consume thousands of CPU hours and cost thousands of dollars. Recursive Self-Improvement via Fast Tree Search (SIFT), a framework from researchers at MIT and Sakana AI, tries to cut that evaluation cost. It uses a separate language model to compare candidate agents before committing to expensive benchmark runs. It can also propose new changes while earlier candidates are still being evaluated. That lets the search explore several branches without waiting for a full test after every patch. On the Polyglot coding benchmark, one SIFT run reached 35.1% accuracy in under five hours of wall-clock time, using 42 CPU hours and about $150 in API credits, according to the researchers. For teams tuning coding-agent harnesses against well-defined tasks, SIFT suggests a way to spend expensive evaluations more selectively rather than running every candidate through the full test suite. ## Every improvement needs a test Engineers can tune a coding agent’s instructions, add tools or change how it responds to failures. But hand-tuning takes expert time and limits the search to ideas people think to try. Recursive self-improvement automates part of that process by allowing the system to modify its own source code. In the self-improvement loop, an agent examines failures and proposes a patch to its harness. The revised agent attempts the target tasks, and its score helps determine which version becomes the starting point for another patch. Because a patch changes the system that will propose or execute later work, improvements can build on one another. Earlier approaches manage this search in different ways. Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM) maintains an archive of agents and checks candidates on increasingly large task sets: first 10 tasks, then 50, with the full Polyglot benchmark held back for final evaluation. The Huxley-Gödel Machine (HGM) considers how an agent and its descendants perform when choosing where to search next. It varies the number of randomly sampled tasks used to evaluate candidates. The main challenge is the cost of testing modifications to the agent harness. In the paper’s cost breakdown, proposing a patch costs about 12 cents. A pairwise judge call costs about 4.4 cents, and SIFT uses up to 10 per candidate, or up to roughly 44 cents. Evaluating an agent on 50 Polyglot tasks costs about $6 and 2.6 CPU hours. Testing a candidate change on just a few tasks is cheap, but its score can be misleading: it may have drawn unusually easy or hard problems. Using a larger test set gives teams a better basis for deciding which version to improve next, but running those extra tasks costs time and money. As the authors put it, the bottleneck is “the poor signal-to-cost trade-off of existing evaluation methods.” ## How SIFT works SIFT builds on DGM’s agent harness but inserts a cheaper source of feedback into the search. Its central bet is that a language model can compare two versions of an agent and judge which is likely to perform better, even before the new candidate completes a large benchmark run. After SIFT generates a modified agent, it runs the new version on four coding tasks. This quick check catches changes that break the agent or leave it unable to solve basic problems, before the system spends more on comparing and testing it. SIFT then asks an LLM-as-a-judge to make pairwise comparisons between the new agent and up to 10 high-ranking agents already in its archive. Comparing two implementations is closer to asking a hiring manager to choose between finalists than asking for an absolute score out of 100. LLMs.titleZh: Cloudflare Clef Decision Models Challenge Jev With Open Weights and an RL Platform
LLMs.content: top of page [Get Download Link for macOS](https://www.remio.ai) [Download remio](https://api.remio.ai/download/installer) # Cloudflare Clef Decision Models Challenge Jev With Open Weights and an RL Platform [Martin Chen](https://www.remio.ai/members-area/d98b79ff-395e-437c-a216-5c4da0100f5428852/profile) 4 hours ago 13 min read Cloudflare released two decision models on October 1, and the larger one already claims a benchmark lead over Jev. The **Cloudflare Clef decision models**, Clef and Clef-flash, return typed probabilities instead of generating unrestricted text. Both are available through Workers AI and as Apache 2.0 licensed weights. That combination creates a direct challenge to TypeSafe AI, which introduced Jev and its System One model category only weeks earlier. Cloudflare adopted Jev’s API format, published competing benchmark results, and added image support. It also connected the models to an emerging reinforcement learning service. The launch is not simply another open model release. Cloudflare wants bounded decisions to become an infrastructure layer for agents, with its network handling inference, data collection, training, and redeployment. Jev established the product pattern, but Cloudflare is trying to turn that pattern into a full platform. The distinction matters because agents make far more decisions than they generate polished answers. They classify requests, choose tools, assess risk, route records, and decide when to ask for help. A model that handles those choices quickly can sit inside the operational path of every automated workflow. Cloudflare’s early numbers support further testing, but they do not settle the market. The evaluations come from the company releasing the models, while its customer fine-tuning platform remains partly hands-on and partly planned. The model is aimed at organisations that want to use AI for software development and modernisation without moving source code, data or workflows outside infrastructure they control. IBM Bob is the company's agentic software development platform, designed to help teams apply AI not only to code generation but also to broader software delivery and modernisation work. The launch comes as large companies increase spending on AI tools for engineering teams while facing tighter internal controls over sensitive data, critical systems and compliance. Those constraints are especially acute in regulated sectors, where data-processing location and AI governance can determine whether a tool can be used at all. The self-hosted version lets customers run the platform where their code, application context and data already reside, rather than transferring them to an external service. **Control demands** IBM is positioning the offering around AI sovereignty and governance, arguing that many customers want closer control over data residency, security rules and operational oversight. That includes environments with limited or intentionally restricted internet connectivity, such as air-gapped systems. Supported models can run on premises, including in isolated environments, using models customers have licensed. Customers can also connect the platform to supported external model services through hybrid configurations. This is particularly relevant for large organisations whose application estates often span older on-premises systems, private clouds and other controlled environments. The deal, whose price was not disclosed, expands Superhuman’s roadmap beyond email productivity into AI safety and authenticity. The acquisition gives Superhuman a proven detection engine and a profitable, lightly‑funded business to integrate into its AI assistant, Superhuman Go. ## Why It Matters The acquisition signals that SaaS leaders are treating AI‑generated content detection as a core product capability rather than a niche add‑on. For operators, the move illustrates a path to diversify revenue by layering trust‑oriented features onto existing workflows, potentially boosting expansion revenue and deepening customer stickiness. For investors, GPTZero’s profitable, low‑capital growth story provides a benchmark for evaluating other AI‑tool startups that aim to monetize compliance and authenticity rather than pure generative functionality. By integrating detection directly into an AI assistant that already spans a million apps, Superhuman can create network effects that amplify both user adoption and data collection, strengthening its competitive moat. The deal also highlights the increasing importance of vertical‑specific AI safety solutions—education, hiring, journalism—where regulatory pressure and brand risk make authenticity a differentiator. ## Key Points 1. AI Product.content: [![](https://assets.bizclikmedia.net/original/42efaea16334d3fe6df5f2ff7ca79136:e38b64b2aac1b5847a4d200a7563cce4/cyber-magazine-light-logo.png)](/ "Home") Article Cyber Security # How Exabeam's Nova AI Triages Cases 30x Faster Than Humans By[Rithula Nisha](/author/rithula-nisha) October 02, 2026 undefined mins Share this article **Prioritise Us** on Google Share this article **Prioritise Us** on Google ![](https://assets.bizclikmedia.net/138/d2e993683425a0b39de052251867e640:41dc75c522650b2f9b2641f01cf81d03/steve-wilson-chief-ai-and-product-officer-exabeam.webp) Steve Wilson, Chief AI and Product Officer at Exabeam | Cybersecurity Excellence Awards Steve Wilson, Chief AI and Product Officer at Exabeam, says the Agentic SOC is "defined by how effectively people and AI agents work together" [Exabeam](https://cybermagazine.com/company/exabeam) is bringing the Agentic SOC to life with new capabilities for its Nova AI, extending AI-driven investigation, execution and governance to cloud and on-premises environments. In the age of [machine-speed attacks](https://cybermagazine.com/news/unit-42-how-ai-agents-breached-a-network-in-10-hours), the company is betting that the future of the SOC is agentic. The behavioural intelligence company notes that the updates are designed to help security teams manage increasingly complex AI-driven threats while keeping human oversight in place. ## What is Exabeam’s Agentic SOC and how does it use AI? The new capabilities build on Exabeam’s work in applied machine learning, user and entity behaviour analytics (UEBA), generative AI and Agent Behaviour Analytics (ABA), which monitors AI agents alongside human users. “The next generation of the SOC won’t be defined by more alerts or more automation. It will be defined by how effectively people and AI agents work together,” says [Steve Wilson](https://cybermagazine.com/executive/steve-wilson-exabeam), Chief AI and Product Officer at Exabeam. ![Youtube Placeholder](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/taOHiPN68bw/hqdefault.jpg) “The SOC was built for a world where humans generated most activity. That world no longer exists. “Today, analysts are defending environments where AI agents can investigate, decide and act at machine speed. “The [Agentic SOC](https://cybermagazine.com/news/diving-into-fortinets-unified-agentic-ai-platform-fortisoc) is the future, where AI accelerates security operations, but people remain responsible for the decisions that matter most.” Nova AI now operates as a persistent investigator across the Exabeam platform, gathering context, running secondary searches and retrieving entity profiles as incidents unfold. Exabeam says its security operations team found that Nova AI triaged an average case in approximately 10 minutes, which is 30 times faster than the usual five hours taken by a human analyst. Related Cases automatically groups connected incidents to give analysts a broader view of activity. The company has also launched the Exabeam Agentic SOC Plugin for Anthropic Claude Code and OpenAI Codex. > The SOC was built for a world where humans generated most activity. That world no longer exists > > Steve Wilson, Chief AI and Product Officer at Exabeam The plugin brings guided workflows into analysts’ AI tools, supporting alert triage, case prioritisation and investigation through natural-language commands. ## How does Exabeam improve AI agent visibility with Claude Enterprise? Exabeam’s deeper Claude Enterprise integration is designed to give security teams visibility into prompts, tool calls and actions through a single timeline. Event-time analysis and behaviour-based correlation can help identify [rogue agents and behavioural drift](https://cybermagazine.com/news/how-rogue-openai-agent-hacked-australia-medicare-system). “The evolution toward an agentic SOC is less about removing analysts from the process and more about changing where their time and judgment are applied,” says Michelle Abraham, Research Vice President, Security and Trust at [ID...

Open Source AI.content: [![Phoronix](/phxcms7-css/phoronix.png)](/) * [Articles & Reviews](/reviews) * [News Archive](/news) * [Forums](/forums/) * [Premium Ad-Free](/phoronix-premium) * [Contact](/contact) * Popular Categories * Close * [Articles & Reviews](/reviews) * [News Archive](/news) * [Forums](/forums/) * [Premium](/phoronix-premium) * [Contact](/contact) * Categories [Computers](/reviews/Computers) [Display Drivers](/reviews/Display+Drivers) [Graphics Cards](/reviews/Graphics+Cards) [Linux Gaming](/reviews/Linux+Gaming) [Memory](/reviews/Memory) [Motherboards](/reviews/Motherboards) [Processors](/reviews/Processors) [Software](/reviews/Software) [Storage](/reviews/Storage) [Operating Systems](/reviews/Operating+Systems) [Peripherals](/reviews/Peripherals) # Apex Compute Developing Open-Source Mesa Vulkan Driver For Their Hardware Written by [Michael Larabel](https://www.michaellarabel.com/) in [Mesa](/linux/Mesa) on 2 October 2026 at 06:17 AM EDT. [1 Comment](/forums/node/1661292) ![MESA](/assets/categories/mesa.webp) Apex Compute is the company started in California in 2024 that aims to produce high-efficiency AI accelerators for real-time edge AI inferencing. So far they have an FPGA prototype for licensing and deployment and carries the bold claim of being "20x faster than the NVIDIA Jetson" and at under 10W and one fifth the cost. Making Apex Compute much more interesting to us now is that they are developing an open-source, Mesa-based Vulkan driver for their hardware. Unlike most of the start-ups running their own half-baked software stacks and a proprietary mess, Apex Compute is developing an open-source Vulkan driver leveraging Mesa. This immediately makes the start-up much more interesting than many others out there. Plus using Vulkan API for AI inferencing opens it up immediately for Llama.cpp and other software with existing Vulkan back-ends rather than having yet another vendor specific interface. Raising my curiosity yesterday was [this Vulkan-Docs merge request](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/Vulkan-Docs/pull/2828) adding the Apex Compute author ID, vendor ID, and driver ID. In that Vulkan merge request they are explicitly clear on being open-source and leveraging Mesa: > "We're building Apex GPU with an open-source Vulkan driver based on Mesa: https://github.com/apex-compute/mesa" Their Mesa branch can be found on [GitHub](https://github.com/apex-compute/mesa). With the Apex Vulkan driver being in active development with many patches as recently as today. It's great as well seeing them develop in the open as well rather than just staged or irregular code dumps to their public repository. It will be interesting to watch as this Apex Vulkan driver develops and hopefully that they'll submit it to upstream Mesa once fully developed. Those curious about Apex Compute now knowing their open-source Mesa Vulkan driver activity can learn more about the start-up at [ApexCompute.com](https://apexcompute.com/). Open Source AI.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) ![](https://img.youtube.com/vi/cKhpeEBnT1o/hqdefault.jpg) [Your Coding Agent Is 6 Months Out of Date — Jakub Hojsan, Exa](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cKhpeEBnT1o) GuestJakub Hojsan 5 hours ago00:12:23en ![](/images/img_default_profile@2x.png)[AI Engineer](/podcast?source=AI%20Engineer) ## Key Takeaways Exa engineer Jakub Hojsan argues coding and review agents need semantic web search with token-efficient highlights to overcome LLM knowledge cutoffs, citing Exa's cost and provider-agnostic advantages. ## Summary Exa's pitch to coding-agent builders rests on a gap that no model release closes: the months between an LLM's training cutoff and the code a review agent is asked to judge. Jakub Hojsan, a forward-deployed engineer at Exa, argues that bolting a web search tool onto an agent is not enough — the model must also be told when to search, and the search itself must return distilled highlights rather than whole pages. The episode is mostly a product-and-architecture talk about semantic search for coding and review agents; the title's "six months out of date" framing is the hook for the first few minutes, after which the discussion moves to token efficiency, transparency, provider neutrality, and Exa's newer Agent offering. Hojsan's core claim is that coding agents do not need "10 blue links." Exa returns context-rich highlights — by his account, roughly 500 characters instead of 100,000 — computed at runtime without an LLM, so no extra latency is added to the search call. He names Cursor, Cognition, Warp, and CodeRabbit as companies using Exa to power web search, and describes a two-step integration pattern: instruct the agent when to search, then execute the search. The briefing below covers the knowledge-cutoff problem, the highlight mechanism, the transparency and cost case against native search tools, the multi-provider argument, the Exa Agent launch with its data partners, and the re-ranking and schema-generation details from the Q&A. ## The knowledge cutoff leaves a review gap no model release closes Hojsan's central problem statement is that every LLM has a knowledge cutoff, and the lag between cutoff date and model release date runs around six months. Anything merged into a repository inside that window is invisible to the model — not just un-creatable as net-new code, but unreviewable. He uses a concrete example: a PR to the Kuder vector store made a few months before the talk, which falls inside the blind spot after GPT-5.5's cutoff date. His contrast is between how a human and a model handle the same diff. A human would go to Stack Overflow, ask whether a variable — in his example, one called "inertia check" — was removed, paste the compile error, get an answer, and open a PR. A model without web search looks at the same diff and concludes it is a cleanup. Hojsan says that reading is wrong: the parameter is being removed because the change is actually a dependency bump requiring a refactor. With web search, the agent can pull the repository itself and any breaking changes from the changelog, then explain the migration in depth. > "Many people without web search will go see, OK, here's the error. The diff looks consistent, and it looks like a cleanup, but that's really not the case." ## Highlights, not pages: 500 characters instead of 100,000 Exa does not return the full GitHub repository page. It returns a small snippet explaining the change. Hojsan describes an interpretation step that distills an entire page down to exactly what the model needs to answer the question — his figure is roughly 500 characters fed to the model instead of 100,000. The mechanism is computational, not generative. Hojsan says Exa pulls specific lines at runtime without using an LLM, which is why the company claims zero added latency on the search call. Open Source AI.content: AWS Strands Labs released an open-source model on Thursday that removes text generation from the agent decision loop entirely. Instead of predicting tokens, Strands Decider 2B reads a situation, compares its hidden-state representation against each candidate answer, and returns a ranked probability list in a median 115 milliseconds on a consumer GPU, according to benchmarks in the package release. The release arrived on the same day Cloudflare shipped its own decision-model pair, Clef and Clef-flash, as described in the Cloudflare announcement post, suggesting the category TypeSafe AI named "System One models" at its September 15 launch is hardening into a recognizable infrastructure tier rather than remaining a single vendor's idea. The model is published at ``` StrandsAgents/strands-decider-2B-hobson-v19 ``` on Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 license, meaning commercial use, modification, and redistribution require no licensing fees. It is installable in one command ( ``` pip install strands-decider ``` ) and comes with a command-line interface and an HTTP server, as confirmed by the package's PyPI listing. No managed hosted inference endpoint exists yet; the bundled server binds to localhost with no authentication layer, which means teams deploying to shared infrastructure need to add access controls themselves. ### What Problem Decision Models Solve in Agent Pipelines An AI agent running in production spends much of its time on decisions that do not require language generation at all: which tool should I call next, is this argument grounded in what the user actually said, does this output meet the requested quality bar, which queue should own this request. Routing each of those through a frontier large language model is slow and expensive by construction — frontier APIs generate text one token at a time whether the task needs a paragraph or a one-word answer. The decision-model category, now represented by Strands Decider 2B, Cloudflare's Clef and Clef-flash, and TypeSafe AI's closed-API Jev, proposes a structural answer detailed in the TypeSafe launch blog: some choices inside an agent loop do not need a language model at all. They need a model that picks reliably from a bounded option set, reports how confident it is, and does so quickly enough to sit on the hot path without becoming the new bottleneck. The TypeSafe team borrowed the term "System One" from cognitive psychologist Daniel Kahneman's framework distinguishing fast, automatic judgment (System 1) from slow, deliberate reasoning (System 2) — though it is worth noting that even Kahneman's collaborator Keith Stanovich has since moved away from the System 1/2 framing as overly simplified. The AI analogy is looser than the marketing suggests, but the engineering problem it describes is real. ### How the Pointer Head Architecture Works The core mechanism of Strands Decider 2B is a departure from standard language-model design. The team took Qwen3.5-2B-Base, a 1.9-billion-parameter decoder model produced by Alibaba's Qwen team and published as open weights, and made a targeted structural change: they removed the language-modeling head — the component responsible for predicting the next word — and replaced it with a pointer head of roughly one million parameters, as described in the project's architecture documentation. That pointer head works by comparing the model's internal representation of the input (captured at a designatedposition in the sequence) against the hidden-state representations of each candidate option's final token. Broadcom is a custom chip and networking leader. If you have $1,000 that you're ready to invest today, that would be enough to start positions in two of the chip stocks that look poised to lead the next wave of the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out in **Advanced Micro Devices**(NASDAQ: AMD) and **Broadcom**(NASDAQ: AVGO). With $1,000, you could buy one share of each. Let's look at why these two [semiconductor stocks](https://www.fool.com/investing/stock-market/market-sectors/information-technology/semiconductor-stocks/?utm_source=globeandmail&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=article&referring_guid=93094985-7367-4b97-869d-45c8768513a9) look like solid investments. ***Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.**In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. [**Continue »**](https://api.fool.com/infotron/infotrack/click?apikey=35527423-a535-4519-a07f-20014582e03e&impression=619bbc8f-82c0-4fbd-b781-56e2e798d533&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.fool.com%2Fmms%2Fmark%2Fa-sa-dd-total-conviction%3Faid%3D11123%26source%3Disaediica0000078%26ftm_cam%3Dsa-dd-4%26ftm_veh%3Dtop_incontent_pitch_feed_partner%26ftm_pit%3D19478&utm_source=globeandmail&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=article&referring_guid=93094985-7367-4b97-869d-45c8768513a9)* ## 1. AMD: An inference, agentic AI, and physical AI winner AMD was outmaneuvered by **Nvidia** in the AI training market, but it's positioning itself to prevent that from happening again. It's developing processors that target the inference, agentic AI, and physical AI markets, and aims to be a viable contender in all three. It has also been making significant investments in memory. This positions it well for the inference market, where architectures that prioritize high volumes of fast memory access are favored over raw compute power. The chiplet design of its graphics processing units (GPUs) allows them to be packaged with more memory, and AMD has also formed a partnership with **Cerebras** to offer a disaggregated inference solution that combines both of their systems. It has also inked a deal to acquire inference chipmaker Taalas, which hardwires AI models directly into its chips. It also bought memory optimization company MEXT earlier this year. And AMD has two $100 billion inference deals in place with OpenAI and **Meta Platforms**, as well as a large agreement with Anthropic. On top of that, the company is a leader in the data center central processing unit (CPU) market. This market has been exploding with the rise of agentic AI, as servers dedicated to powering AI agents require considerably more CPUs than those used for AI training. AMD forecasts that the data center CPU market will grow to $220 billion in the coming years, although in light of the rapidly growing popularity of Meta's new Muse agentic AI offering, this estimate could prove low. Meta, by the way, is running its Muse agents on AMD's CPUs. Finally, with its agreement to acquire AI model and research lab World Labs, AMD is improving its ability to pursue the physical AI and robotics markets. World Lab's expertise lies in spatial intelligence models, and it will provide AMD with the tools to advance an open AI ecosystem (in contrast to Nvidia's closed system) that serves those emerging AI markets. This deal isn't about selling more chips in the near term, but rather about creating future architectures and platforms for physical AI. Given all its opportunities for growth ahead, AMD stock is a buy. ![AMD and Broadcom logos.](https://barchart-news-media-prod.aws.barchart.com/FC/e0d2edd172dd97f7acbf3942...

Their ClusterMAX 3.0 ranking of 323 GPU cloud providers — up from about 120 in the first edition — finds security remains the sector's worst failure, with one cluster exposing national intelligence data to outside testers. The bar for a top-tier cloud has risen to deploying NVIDIA's GB300 NVL72 rack-scale system, a shift that demoted several former leaders. Patel argues that Google DeepMind is becoming compute-poorer than OpenAI and Anthropic as GCP sells capacity to would-be rivals, and that NVIDIA's Poolside and Hugging Face deals are defensive moves to keep critical talent and ecosystem assets out of competitors' hands. The report also covers the structural coverage gap in cloud rankings, the blurring line between training and inference, and SemiAnalysis's plan to extend testing beyond NVIDIA silicon. ##### Key Elements ![Dylan Patel: GPU Access for AI Startups Is the Hardest Ever as Inference Margins Hit 60%](https://img.biggo.com/DmFtehRRNdHlEOj_wQJgavxfyX7TlP2m25Ymw2AratM/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwL2I4ZDk4MzQ4MjA2NzAzZWFfMTc5MDk2Mjk2Ml9jb3Zlci5qcGc.webp) Inference providers have become so profitable that they are now outbidding the very AI labs they were built to serve. That single shift — from roughly 10% gross margins nine months ago to around 60% now on open models — has made GPU access the hardest it has ever been for new startups, according to Dylan Patel, co-founder of SemiAnalysis, speaking on the Latent Space podcast. Patel and his colleague Jordan, who runs the firm's ClusterMAX testing program, used the episode to walk through the third edition of their neocloud ranking. But the ranking itself is a lens on a much bigger story: the economics of AI compute have flipped, the security of GPU clouds is disturbingly weak, and the industry's biggest players are making defensive moves that will shape who gets to build frontier models. ### Security is the sector's worst failure, and the checks are basic The most alarming content in SemiAnalysis's work isn't about performance benchmarks. It's about who can see your data. In the first ClusterMAX, testers found they could see other tenants' jobs, data, and repositories because providers had not implemented network security controls properly. SemiAnalysis reported the finding to the offending company and to NVIDIA, then rated the firm poorly. The second version found similar problems. The third version found serious issues again — so serious that SemiAnalysis published a newsletter titled "Most Neo-Clouds Are Terrible at Security," which prompted OpenAI co-founder Ilya Sutskever to tweet hours later that security at most neoclouds is useless. Patel described one case where testers could see national intelligence data belonging to a country, with several national security agencies and military intelligence units working in the same neocloud. "Imagine if we had evil intentions," he said. The company fixed the issue, but Patel argues SemiAnalysis should not be the party responsible for checking whether a provider is secure — even though the industry apparently needs exactly that service. Jordan stressed that the technical checks involved are not sophisticated. They include verifying current software versions, updated drivers, and correct configuration. Infra & Chips.content: ![]() ![GuruFocus](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/gurufocus--theme-light.svg) ![GuruFocus](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/gurufocus--theme-dark.svg) # Broadcom Is Lining Up $60 Billion to Fuel the AI Chip Race Against Nvidia ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/broadcom.svg) Broadcom Inc. (AVGO, Financials), the chip and infrastructure software company, could get another boost from the artificial intelligence spending boom as Wall Street works to assemble $60 billion in financing for chips and data-center equipment used by Anthropic and other AI companies. The size of the package is notable even by the standards of the current AI buildout. Banks are preparing to syndicate $42 billion of senior-secured debt, according to the report. Blackstone is leading another $18 billion of junior debt and plans to provide $9 billion from its own funds before syndicating the rest. For Broadcom, the financing could help turn demand for AI computing into additional chip and equipment sales. The company has been expanding its position in AI infrastructure, putting it in more direct competition with Nvidia for a growing pool of data-center spending. But there is another side to the story. Building AI infrastructure increasingly depends on enormous amounts of outside capital. That makes lenders' willingness to fund these projects almost as important as demand for the technology itself. The $60 billion package therefore offers investors a useful test of both Broadcom's AI opportunity and Wall Street's appetite for financing it. The next thing to watch is whether the debt package attracts enough demand to move forward as planned. ## [AVGO chart](/chart/?symbol=NASDAQ%3AAVGO) ## [Latest news](/news-flow) ## [More news from GuruFocus](/news-flow/?provider=gurufocus) Select market data provided by [ICE Data Services](https://www.ice.com/fixed-income-data-services). As U.S. export controls on advanced AI semiconductors to China have made it increasingly difficult to procure high-performance chips on the Chinese mainland, Tencent has adopted a workaround strategy of renting overseas data center computing capacity. Alibaba and ByteDance have also established themselves as major customers of Southeast Asian data centers, driving demand for data center construction and high-value memory products including HBM, server DRAM, and enterprise SSDs. Tencent's second-quarter capital expenditure surged 176% year-over-year, while its free cash flow turned negative for the first time in about a decade. Chinese Big Tech companies are continuing aggressive AI investment, in stark contrast to the AI slowdown debate unfolding in the United States. ##### Key Elements ![Tencent Signs $7 Billion Deal with Oracle—China's AI Takes a Detour Through Southeast Asian Data Centers](https://img.biggo.com/HIxQ8OrD0W04GuGXhwj7s4hqvjX6UqLJFSITzvJWh3I/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwLzViZjdjMzRhLWE4MTAtNDJhMS04Yzg2LTkxOTM4MjBlMTllMl8xNzkwOTMxNjAwX2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) China's largest IT company, Tencent, has reportedly signed a five-year computing resource lease agreement with U.S. cloud provider Oracle worth approximately $7 billion (about 9.4 trillion won). Amid intensifying U.S. export controls on advanced AI semiconductors to China, Tencent is pursuing AI model development and service expansion by renting high-performance AI chips—which are difficult to secure on the Chinese mainland—from Southeast Asian data centers. According to a Financial Times report on the 2nd, this deal is the largest overseas computing resource lease agreement Tencent has ever signed. Tencent will gain access to approximately 100,000 advanced AI chips across Oracle's data centers in multiple Southeast Asian locations for five years, and is reported to have paid roughly 30% of the contract value upfront. Tencent and Oracle have not issued official statements regarding the reports. ### Regulatory Barriers, Circumvented Beyond Borders The United States has continuously tightened export controls to prevent Nvidia's high-performance AI chips from reaching China through third countries. As direct procurement of advanced AI accelerators on the Chinese mainland has become increasingly difficult, Chinese Big Tech companies have pivoted toward renting computing capacity from chips installed in overseas data centers. Leasing computing resources from overseas data centers falls outside the direct scope of current U.S. regulations. As a result, Alibaba and ByteDance have already established themselves as major customers in the Southeast Asian data center market, and with Tencent now joining with a large-scale contract, lease prices, contract durations, and upfront payment amounts are all trending upward together. The computing resources secured by Tencent are expected to be deployed toward enhancing the performance of its proprietary AI model "Hunyuan" and expanding AI agent services. Tencent is accelerating efforts to transform WeChat—its messaging platform with over 1.4 billion users—into an AI agent platform. With millions of mini-programs connected to WeChat, enabling AI to directly invoke these services could create a large-scale agent ecosystem that connects natural language commands to real transactions and service execution. #...
